meaning.text: Machal glosses the Poludnica, or Polednica, as "Midday Spirit".
Afanasyev derives the name of the poludnitsy from poldenʹ, "midday", which he glosses as the south, the warm, summer side.
Ralston, saying she appears exactly at mid-day, gives the Russian for mid-day as Polden or Poluden, "half-day".

scene.text: She appears in the fields, usually at the time of harvest.
In Bohemian tradition she wanders about the fields at noon.
In Polish belief she stays during the summer either in the fields or in the woods.
Among the Lusatians she appears in the fields exactly at mid-day.
Among the Lusatians she walks over the fields from twelve to two o'clock.
The Russians tell of her walking about the fields at harvest-time and seizing those she finds working there at midday.
In Archangel Government she is spoken of as being in the rye.

appearance.text: According to Bohemian tradition she has the appearance of an airy, white lady.
According to Bohemian tradition she may instead appear as an old woman.
Sometimes she is slight and slim like a girl twelve years old.
In that girlish form she has a whip in her hand.

behavior_habitat.text: She haunts the dwellings of men.
She floats high up in the air amid violent gusts of wind.
Whomsoever she touches will die a sudden death.
She strikes with her whip anyone who crosses her path, and such a man is doomed to an early death.
She is peculiarly fond of ambushing women who have recently borne children and who go out into the street at midday.
A child left alone in the fields at harvest-time may be stolen by a Poludnica.
Crying children are hushed by the threat that she will come and carry them away.
In the forest regions of Bohemia people tell of forest poludnitsy who at noon fly in whirling whirlwinds.
These forest poludnitsy of Bohemia steal small children.
Among the Czechs the poludnitsa is called a forest woman who roams the fields at midday.
Among the Czechs she exchanges small children whom peasant women leave unattended for her own.
The stolen child fares well or badly according to how the family treats the changeling.

According to folk tradition, as midnight has its evil beings so does noon, and these exercise their destructive power especially from eleven to twelve o'clock; they are called poludnice, or more generally wild women.

appearance.text: In Moravia she is represented as an old woman.
In Moravia she is clad in a white gown.
In Moravia she is said to have horses' hoofs.
In Moravia she has an ugly face.
In Moravia she has slanting eyes.
In Moravia she has dishevelled hair.
In Polish belief she manifests herself in the shape of a tall woman.
She is dressed in a white robe reaching to her feet.
She carries a sharp sickle in her hand.

behavior_habitat.text: During the summer she gives chase to the people who work in the fields or woods.
Frequently she propounds hard questions to them, and if they are unable to answer she sends grievous maladies upon them.
Sometimes she appears in cottages during a storm.
The peasants ascribe various natural phenomena to her, such as the fata morgana.
When she leaves the fields or the forests she is accompanied by seven great black dogs.
Women and children are her favourite victims.

appearance.text: Among the Lusatian Serbs she is represented as a tall old woman.
Among the Lusatian Serbs she may instead be represented as a young female.
She wears a white gown.
She holds a sickle in her hand.

behavior_habitat.text: Among the Lusatian Serbs she is the subject of many stories.
Coming out of the woods at midday, she appears to those who may be working there.
She addresses any woman whom she finds tarrying afield instead of returning home for the mid-day rest.
She stops unexpectedly before anyone who lingers at field work at noon.
She puts questions about the growing of flax and hemp and punishes those who are unable to answer.
She questions women on the cultivation and the spinning of flax.
She asks in detail how flax is worked and how yarn and linen are prepared.
She cuts off the head or divides the neck of an unsatisfactory answerer.
Those who cannot answer her questions have their heads wrung, or are at least punished with a grave illness.
She wrings the necks of women who cannot tell her how flax should be worked.
The Lusatian poludnitsa punishes with death anyone who cannot answer her intricate questions.
Her most usual victims are young women who either have children at home or are still in childbed.
At noon she guards the corn from thieves.
She punishes children who tread upon the ears of corn.
There is a Lusatian saying, "she questions like a pripolnica".

appearance.text: The Russians believe that she has the shape of a tall and beautiful girl.
In Russian belief she is dressed in a white gown.

behavior_habitat.text: She lures small children into the corn.
Walking about the fields at harvest-time, she seizes the heads of those she finds working there at midday and twists their necks, causing them violent pain.
In other parts of Russia she appears as guardian of fields.
In Archangel Government the poludnitsa is the guardian of fields sown with rye.
In Archangel Government parents frighten children with "Don't go into the rye, the poludnitsa will burn you!" or "The poludnitsa will eat you!"
Afanasyev says that in Russia only weak and fragmentary memories of the poludnitsy have survived.

appearance.text: The Siberian Russians picture her as an old woman.
She has thick, curly hair.
In southern Siberia she has thick, dishevelled hair.
She wears scanty clothing.
In southern Siberia she is dressed in rags.

behavior_habitat.text: She lives among the reeds or in the dense thickets of nettles.
In southern Siberia she lives in the bath-house or in nettle bushes.
She kidnaps naughty children.
In southern Siberia she guards kitchen gardens from mischievous children.

dealing_with_it.text: Among the Lusatian Serbs anyone she meets in the fields at midday must talk with her for fully an hour about one and the same thing; those who fail either forfeit their heads or have some illness sent upon them.
Among the Czechs, people dislike walking in the woods at exactly noon, lest a wild woman send bewilderment upon them.

notes.text: appearance (top level): left empty because every physical description in the sources is tied to one people or region (Bohemia, Moravia, Poles, Lusatian Serbs, Russians, Siberian Russians) and the descriptions differ (white lady, old woman, girl of twelve, tall woman, tall beautiful girl, old woman in rags); they are recorded in the variants. Searched poludnitsa, poludnica, polednica, polednice, poludnice, prezpolnica, pripolnica, pripoldnica, przypoludnica, midday spirit, полудница, полудницы, полудниц, полудн in all sources.
behavior_habitat (top level): left empty because every behaviour the sources give is tied to a specific people or region; see the variants. Same searches as for appearance.

origin: no opened page says where a poludnitsa comes from or who becomes one. Afanasyev offers only mythological interpretation (see the scope note). Searched the name terms above plus полуденн, полдень, poledne, midday, noon, field-spirit.

Afanasyev interprets the poludnitsy as identical with the sun-maidens of Serbian songs and the white women of German sagas (vol. 3 p.137), as belonging to the same class of spirits as the Serbian vily (vol. 3 pp.76-77), and as a cloud-maiden once given oversight of flax fields (vol. 3 p.139). Ralston says she seems akin to the daemon Meridianus (p.148). These are the authors' comparative theories, not reported belief, so none of them was entered as origin or behaviour.

related rusalka: Afanasyev vol. 3 p.139 says tradition ascribes the same traits to the rusalki, and vol. 1 p.23 compares the Lusatian poludnitsa's deadly questions with the riddles of the rusalki. This is a comparison by the author, recorded as 'related' only.

erben1893 is a literary source. Only Erben's prose note on folk belief (p.183) was used. His poem 'Polednice' (pp.45-47), in which a mother calls the polednice on her crying child and the child is found smothered at the stroke of noon, describes her as small, brown, wild-faced, under a kerchief, on a crutch, with crooked shanks and a voice like a whirlwind; none of this was entered as appearance or behaviour because it is a poet's literary depiction.

Afanasyev vol. 3 p.138 notes that priestless Old Believers say a prayer at noon to drive out the 'noonday demon' (бѣса полуденна). The page places this in the poludnitsa passage but does not say the prayer is against the poludnitsa, so it was not entered under dealing_with_it.

OCR: Machal p.267 prints the Polish forms as 'Pofudnica (Potudniowka, Przypoludnica)'; the variants record them without diacritics as Poludniowka and Przypoludnica, and the garbled 'Pofudnica' is not recorded separately. Afanasyev's Latin-script Czech and Lusatian forms (e.g. 'роіесіпісе', 'ргіроіпіса') are OCR-garbled and were not copied as native names. 'Sorbs' is used for Machal's 'Lusatian Serbs' and Ralston's 'Lusatians'; Moravia is recorded under Czechs. The tag afanasyev1865:p.23 resolves to a page whose printed number reads 25.
